Decision Tree In-Class Exercise: Customer Churn Prediction

Ralchukwu Mogbogu

2025-11-05

Introduction

Welcome to the Decision Tree in-class exercise! In this exercise, you will apply the concepts learned in today’s lecture to build and evaluate decision tree models for predicting customer churn.

Scenario: You are working as a data scientist for a telecommunications company. The company is experiencing customer churn (customers leaving the service) and wants to predict which customers are likely to churn so they can take proactive retention measures.

Dataset: customer_churn_data.csv contains information about 300 customers with the following variables: - CustomerID: Unique identifier - Age: Customer age - TenureMonths: How long the customer has been with the company - MonthlyCharges: Monthly subscription fee - TotalCharges: Total amount charged to the customer - ContractType: Type of contract (Month-to-Month, One Year, Two Year) - InternetService: Type of internet service (DSL, Fiber Optic, No) - TechSupport: Whether customer has tech support (Yes/No) - OnlineSecurity: Whether customer has online security (Yes/No) - NumSupportCalls: Number of support calls made - Churn: Target variable - Did the customer churn? (Yes/No)

Time: 40 minutes

Section 1: Data Preparation and Exploration (8 minutes)

1.1 Load Required Libraries

Load the necessary libraries for this exercise.

# Load required libraries
# YOUR CODE HERE
library(readxl)
library(caret)
library(dplyr)

library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(Metrics)

Question 1.1: How many customers are in the dataset? How many features (excluding CustomerID and Churn)?

Your Answer: Since the Tibble shows “300 x 11,” the number of customers will be 300, as in 300 rows of customers in the data. The features are 11 (variables) in total, so if we exclude CustomerID and Churn, we are left with 9. Therefore, there are 300 customers and 9 features

Question 1.2: What is the distribution of the target variable Churn? What percentage of customers churned?

Your Answer:

# distribution

distr <- table(df$Churn)
print ("distribution of the target variable `Churn`:")
## [1] "distribution of the target variable `Churn`:"
print(distr)
## 
##  No Yes 
## 183 117
# percentage customers churned
print("percentage of customers churned:")
## [1] "percentage of customers churned:"
print((distr/300) * 100)
## 
##  No Yes 
##  61  39

Your Answer: Among 300 customers, the distrubition of the target variable “Churn” is 117 Yes and 183 No. By that reseoning to find of the percentage of customers churned, the Yes frequency is divided by the total 300 and multiplied by 100; i.e, (117/300)*100, which will give a value of 39. Therefore, the percentage of customers churned is 39%

1.3 Data Preprocessing

Convert categorical variables to factors and split the data into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets.

sum(is.na(df)) # no missing values
## [1] 0
# Remove CustomerID as it's not useful for prediction
# YOUR CODE HERE


df_new <- df[, !names(df) %in% "CustomerID"]


# Convert categorical variables to factors
# YOUR CODE HERE
catVariables <- names(df_new)[sapply(df_new, is.character)]
str(catVariables)
##  chr [1:5] "ContractType" "InternetService" "TechSupport" "OnlineSecurity" ...
df_new[catVariables] <- lapply(df_new[catVariables], as.factor)
str(df_new)
## tibble [300 × 10] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
##  $ Age            : num [1:300] 19 24 66 62 64 65 29 49 58 41 ...
##  $ TenureMonths   : num [1:300] 34 41 17 12 58 5 22 30 46 47 ...
##  $ MonthlyCharges : num [1:300] 56.4 46.3 113.5 67.1 84.6 ...
##  $ TotalCharges   : num [1:300] 1798 1825 2006 886 4846 ...
##  $ ContractType   : Factor w/ 3 levels "Month-to-Month",..: 1 1 1 1 1 3 1 2 2 1 ...
##  $ InternetService: Factor w/ 3 levels "DSL","Fiber Optic",..: 2 1 1 3 3 2 3 2 1 2 ...
##  $ TechSupport    : Factor w/ 2 levels "No","Yes": 1 2 2 2 1 2 2 1 1 2 ...
##  $ OnlineSecurity : Factor w/ 2 levels "No","Yes": 1 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 1 ...
##  $ NumSupportCalls: num [1:300] 0 2 2 2 1 5 2 1 3 1 ...
##  $ Churn          : Factor w/ 2 levels "No","Yes": 1 1 1 1 2 2 1 2 2 1 ...
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(530)

# Create training and testing sets (70/30 split)
# YOUR CODE HERE

X <- df_new[, -ncol(df_new)]
Y <- df_new$Churn

train_index <- createDataPartition(Y, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

X_train <- X[train_index, ]
X_test  <- X[-train_index, ]
y_train <- Y[train_index]
y_test  <- Y[-train_index]

# Verify the split
# YOUR CODE HERE

# check the size for both training and testing 
cat("Training:", nrow(X_train), "\n")
## Training: 211
cat("Testing:", nrow(X_test), "\n\n")
## Testing: 89
cat("\nTraining Class:\n")
## 
## Training Class:
print(prop.table(table(y_train)) * 100)
## y_train
##       No      Yes 
## 61.13744 38.86256
cat("Testing Class:\n")
## Testing Class:
print(prop.table(table(y_test)) * 100)
## y_test
##       No      Yes 
## 60.67416 39.32584

Question 1.3: How many observations are in your training set and testing set?

Your Answer: Using the stratified sampling method, we obtained 211 training and 89 testing observations. This approach is necessary to maintain class balance in the churn and prevents bias caused by class imbalance.

Section 2: Building Your First Decision Tree (10 minutes)

2.1 Build a Basic Decision Tree

Build a decision tree using the rpart package with default settings.

# Build a decision tree with default parameters
# YOUR CODE HERE
trainData <- cbind(X_train, Churn=y_train)
testData <- cbind(X_test,  Churn = y_test)

treemodel <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = trainData, method = "class")

# Print the tree summary
# YOUR CODE HERE

print(treemodel)

Question 2.1: What is the root node split? Which variable was chosen first and why do you think this variable was selected?

Your Answer: The root node split will be the fist split in the decision tree which is Node 1. The variable chosen first is TenureMonths du3e to its <6.5 split

2.2 Visualize the Decision Tree

Create a visualization of your decision tree.

# Visualize the tree using rpart.plot
# YOUR CODE HERE


rpart.plot(
  x = treemodel,                 # the decision tree object
  type = 2,                      # structure/label layout
  extra = +104,                # automatically choose info shown at nodes
  under = FALSE,                 # show text inside boxes, not underneath
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,          # align leaves at the bottom neatly
  digits = 2,                    # round numeric labels to 2 digits
  varlen = 0,                    # show full variable names
  faclen = 0,                    # show full factor level names
  roundint = TRUE,               # round splits if all values are integers
  cex = 0.9,                    # auto text size
  tweak = 1.2,                   # slightly enlarge text (like zoom)
  box.palette = "auto",          # auto-select color palette (like filled=True)
  shadow.col = 0,                # no box shadow (0 = off)
  main = "Decision Tree for Customer Churn"
)

Question 2.2: How many leaf nodes does your tree have? What is the maximum depth of the tree?

Your Answer: There are 10 leaf nodes and the max depth is 6

2.3 Variable Importance

Examine which variables are most important for the decision tree.

# Display variable importance
# YOUR CODE HERE

df_varImportance <- data.frame(importance = treemodel$variable.importance)
df_varImportance
##                 importance
## TotalCharges    15.9110618
## TenureMonths    14.2093649
## NumSupportCalls  9.1224425
## Age              6.4223177
## TechSupport      5.4744060
## MonthlyCharges   3.4605014
## ContractType     1.5691832
## OnlineSecurity   0.7792404
## InternetService  0.3138366
# Create a variable importance plot
# YOUR CODE HERE

df2 <- df_varImportance %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "variable") %>%
  arrange(importance) %>%
  mutate(variable = forcats::fct_inorder(variable))

# variable importance plot 

ggplot(df2) +
  geom_col(aes(x = variable, y = importance),
           col='black', show.legend = F) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Variable Importance from Decision Tree",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Importance Score"
  ) + scale_fill_grey() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)

Question 2.3: List the top 3 most important variables according to your model. Do these make business sense for predicting churn?

Your Answer: These are the top 3 most importance variables based on our tree model.

# Create confusion matrix

# Display the confusion matrix
# YOUR CODE HERE

# converting new confusion matrix to data frame
conf_matrix_df <- as.data.frame(conf_matrix$table)
colnames(conf_matrix_df) <- c("Predicted", "Actual", "Freq")

# Reorder the factor levels so that "Yes" comes before "No"
conf_matrix_df$Predicted <- factor(conf_matrix_df$Predicted, levels = c("Yes", "No"))
conf_matrix_df$Actual <- factor(conf_matrix_df$Actual, levels = c("No","Yes"))

# confusion matrix using ggplot2
ggplot2::ggplot(conf_matrix_df, aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() + 
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), color = "black", size = 5, fontface="bold") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14)
    ) + theme_bw() + coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Confusion Matrix for the Decision Tree Model",
    x = "Predicted",
    y = "Actual"
  )

3.3 Calculate Performance Metrics

Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

# Calculate metrics from confusion matrix
# YOUR CODE HERE
# Ensure both actual and predicted are factors with same level order

compare_df_metrics <- compare_df

compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values <- ifelse(compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values == "Yes", 1, 0)
compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values    <- ifelse(compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values == "Yes", 1, 0)


recall_val = recall(compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values, compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values)
precision_val = precision(compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values, compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values)
f1_score = f1(compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values, compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values)
acc_val = accuracy(compare_df_metrics$Actual_Values, compare_df_metrics$Predicted_Values)

# Print all metrics
# YOUR CODE HERE

cat("Recall:", recall_val, "\n")
## Recall: 0.4
cat("Precision:", precision_val, "\n")
## Precision: 0.4242424
cat("F1-score:", f1_score, "\n")
## F1-score: 1
cat("Accuracy:", acc_val, "\n")
## Accuracy: 0.5505618

Question 3.2: What is the accuracy of your model? What does this tell you about the model’s performance?

Your Answer:

The model currently has an accuracy of 55.05%. This figure does not provide strong evidence of predictive performance, as it appears to predict churn status for over half of the customers in the test set. Although it is slightly above the fifty percent mark, it cannot be considered a reliable model for predicting churn status within the system. It fails to adequately capture the relationships between the independent variables and the dependent variables. This summarizes the current situation.

Question 3.3: Which is higher - precision or recall? What does this imply about your model’s behavior (does it make more false positive or false negative errors)?

Your Answer:

The model achieved a higher precision than recall, currently 0.42 and 0.4, respectively, indicating that the model was slightly better at minimizing false positives, predicting 42% of the cases identified as churn. However, it struggles with true positives, as it misses about 60% of actual churn cases, with a recall of only 40%. This discrepancy between precision and recall highlights an imbalance in the model’s performance, making it less effective at distinguishing between churn and non-churn customers.

Section 4: Controlling Tree Complexity (10 minutes)

4.1 Build Trees with Different Complexity Parameters

Build three decision trees with different cp (complexity parameter) values to see how it affects the tree.

# Tree with low cp (more complex tree)
# YOUR CODE HERE
# Source - https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37721047/selecting-cp-value-for-decision-tree-pruning-using-rpart
# Posted by Alan Chalk
# Retrieved 2025-11-05, License - CC BY-SA 3.0

printcp(treemodel)
## 
## Classification tree:
## rpart(formula = Churn ~ ., data = trainData, method = "class")
## 
## Variables actually used in tree construction:
## [1] Age             ContractType    NumSupportCalls TechSupport    
## [5] TenureMonths    TotalCharges   
## 
## Root node error: 82/211 = 0.38863
## 
## n= 211 
## 
##        CP nsplit rel error  xerror     xstd
## 1 0.18293      0   1.00000 1.00000 0.086347
## 2 0.12195      1   0.81707 0.92683 0.085039
## 3 0.02439      2   0.69512 0.89024 0.084265
## 4 0.01000      8   0.50000 0.84146 0.083102
treemodel1 <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = trainData, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.18))

# Tree with moderate cp
# YOUR CODE HERE

treemodel2 <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = trainData, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.12))


# Tree with high cp (simpler tree)
# YOUR CODE HERE

treemodel3 <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = trainData, method = "class", control = rpart.control(cp = 0.02))


# Visualize all three trees
# YOUR CODE HERE


rpart.plot(
  x = treemodel1,                 # the decision tree object
  type = 2,                      # structure/label layout
  extra = +104,                # automatically choose info shown at nodes
  under = FALSE,                 # show text inside boxes, not underneath
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,          # align leaves at the bottom neatly
  digits = 2,                    # round numeric labels to 2 digits
  varlen = 0,                    # show full variable names

Question 4.2: Which tree has the best test accuracy? Is it the most complex tree? What does this tell you about overfitting?

Section 5: Pruning and Cross-Validation (4 minutes)

5.1 Find Optimal CP Using Cross-Validation

Use cross-validation to find the optimal complexity parameter.

# Build a full tree
# YOUR CODE HERE

set.seed(12)

train_control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 2) # 10 partitions, and repeat twice

gridTune <- expand.grid(cp = seq(0.001, 0.05, by = 0.01)) # parameters of the model 

cross_ValTree <- train(Churn ~ ., 
                        data = trainData, 
                        method = "rpart",
                        trControl = train_control,
                        tuneGrid = gridTune,
                        maxdepth = 5,
                        minbucket = 5)



# Display the cp table
# YOUR CODE HERE
print(cross_ValTree$results)
##      cp  Accuracy     Kappa AccuracySD   KappaSD
## 1 0.001 0.6344156 0.2237205 0.08476364 0.1902460
## 2 0.011 0.6391775 0.2191561 0.07466451 0.1710102
## 3 0.021 0.6608442 0.2376740 0.05758706 0.1582657
## 4 0.031 0.6516558 0.2124149 0.06542763 0.1685178
## 5 0.041 0.6585823 0.2290235 0.05765204 0.1424931
# Plot cross-validation results
# YOUR CODE HERE
plot(cross_ValTree)

# Find the best cp value
# YOUR CODE HERE
best_cp_CV = cross_ValTree$bestTune
cat("Best CP value based on cross-validation:", best_cp_CV$cp, "\n")
## Best CP value based on cross-validation: 0.021

Question 5.1: What is the optimal cp value according to cross-validation? What is the cross-validation error at this point?

Your Answer: Optimal cp was 0.02 based on higher accuracy of 66.08%. This corresponds to a cross validation error of approximately 0.339 i.e., 34%

5.2 Prune the Tree

Prune the tree using the optimal cp value.

# Prune the tree using optimal cp
# YOUR CODE HERE

best_cp =  best_cp_CV$cp

#prune_tree =  prune(tree_full, cp = best_cp)

pruned_tree <- cross_ValTree$finalModel


# Visualize the pruned tree
# YOUR CODE HERE
rpart.plot(pruned_tree, type = 2, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           main = sprintf("Pruned Tree (cp = %.2f)", best_cp))

# Evaluate pruned tree on test set
# YOUR CODE HERE
#pruned_pred_class <- predict(pruned_tree, newdata = X_test, type = "class")
pruned_pred_class <- predict(cross_ValTree, newdata = X_test)


pruned_df <- data.frame(
  Actual_Values = y_test,
  Predicted_Values = pruned_pred_class
)

# Converting Yes/No to 1/0
pruned_df$Actual_Values <- ifelse(pruned_df$Actual_Values == "Yes", 1, 0)
pruned_df$Predicted_Values <- ifelse(pruned_df$Predicted_Values == "Yes", 1, 0)

prune_acc <- accuracy(pruned_df$Actual_Values, pruned_df$Predicted_Values)
cat(sprintf("Test Accuracy (cp = %.2f): %.2f%%\n", best_cp, prune_acc*100))
## Test Accuracy (cp = 0.02): 60.67%

Question 5.2: Did pruning improve or hurt the test set performance compared to your original tree? By how much?

Your Answer: It improved the model, so it did not hurt the test set performance, it had an accuracy of 60.67% compared to the baseline model of 55.06%. It increased by 5.61%

Section 6: Reflection and Conclusions (Optional - if time permits)

Question 6.1: Based on your analysis, which customers are most at risk of churning? What business recommendations would you make to reduce churn?

Your Answer: The pruned decision tree, optimized with a complexity parameter (cp) of 0.02, emerged as the definitive model following rigorous cross-validation. This model demonstrates a cross-validated accuracy of approximately 66% and a test accuracy of 60.67%, indicating moderate predictive performance. Analysis derived from this model reveals that customer segments characterized by low tenure, minimal total charges, frequent support calls, younger age demographics, and the lack of technical support are particularly vulnerable to churn. To address this challenge, I propose leveraging the effectiveness of personalized nudges tailored to each customer. Given the complexities of user behavior, it is imperative to implement strategies rooted in the Fogg Behavior Model, which emphasizes the interplay of motivation, ability, and triggers. By enhancing engagement through this structured approach, we can significantly reduce churn rates.

Question 6.2: What are the limitations of using decision trees for this problem? How might you address these limitations?

Your Answer: One drawback of using a decision tree for this classification problem is that it can easily overfit, especially given the small number of observations in this study.
